overview.intro: An extract from Cronin’s novel The Citadel, the story compresses one night’s work into a sequence of mounting difficulty: Andrew Manson, newly out of medical school, is called late to the Morgan house, where after a long labour the baby is born lifeless and the mother’s life is in danger. The unit follows his clinical sequence step by step, studies how suspense is built through procedure rather than through melodrama, and examines the moment at which the night’s work becomes, for him, a vocation rather than a job.

learn.title: The call: night, the Morgan house and a distracted doctor

blocks.text: The story opens on interruption: late at night Andrew Manson is called to the Morgan house, where Susan Morgan is in labour with her first child after twenty years of marriage. Manson is newly out of medical school and beginning his practice in a small mining town, so the case arrives at the least convenient moment and at the start of a career. The setting does two jobs at once — the hour and the isolation of a small-town night narrow the options available, and the household itself, with its midwife and Susan’s mother keeping watch, establishes the audience whose reactions will register every stage of what follows.

Manson is also not entirely free for the work: he arrives with personal preoccupations weighing on him, distracted and weary, and the story’s first movement is the setting aside of all that in favour of the task in front of him. This matters for the ending, because the night’s achievement is presented as something that reorders his priorities rather than merely exercises his skill. The narration stays close to him throughout — we are given his observations, his assessments and his doubts rather than an objective record — which is why the suspense binds: the reader knows only what he notices.

learn.title: Stillbirth: the mother first, then the lifeless child

blocks.text: After a long and difficult labour the baby is born lifeless, and almost at once the second emergency supersedes the first: Susan is in danger too. Manson’s response is clinically ordered and worth following closely — he attends the mother first, using an injection to bring her back from the critical point, and only then turns his full attention to the child. The sequencing is the story’s quiet display of professionalism: in a crisis he does not choose the more dramatic patient but the one whose danger is immediate and treatable, and he returns to the baby with his hands free and his priorities settled.

The child, meanwhile, has been given up on by everyone else. The midwife, practical and experienced, sees the baby pale and still and loses hope; Susan’s mother can only wait and pray; the room settles into the atmosphere of a house that has accepted a death. Against that settling Manson begins work — hot and cold water baths, chest compression, artificial respiration — and keeps it up for over thirty minutes while the evidence stays against him. The construction is classic procedural suspense: the reader is given methods, durations and failure rather than exclamations, and the pressure comes from the gap between effort and result.

learn.title: The cry, the title and “something real at last”

blocks.text: At the point when Manson is about to give up, the child shows signs of life and begins to cry, and the room’s despair converts to relief and tears. Manson’s own reaction is the story’s true ending: emotionally overwhelmed, he realises that he has done something real at last. The line is doing two things — it registers the immediate triumph of the moment, and it settles a question the story has been carrying about what his work is for. Everything personal he arrived with is momentarily answered by something he can stand beside.

That is why the title works in two directions. On the literal level the chapter records a birth: a child brought into the world against the odds. On the other level it records Manson’s own — the moment a young doctor discovers the satisfaction his profession can give, which the story presents as a beginning rather than an achievement. Examination answers should hold both senses together and support each with the text: the baby’s cry for the first, the closing words and his emotional reaction for the second. The restraint matters too — the story does not end with praise or reward, only with a man alone with what he has done, which is why the scene reads as conviction rather than triumphalism.

blocks.text: The story is a model of procedural suspense, and its devices are transferable to any examination of tension. First, it limits the field: one house, one night, a small town with no help to summon, so every minute narrows the options. Second, it withholds comfort — the midwife’s hopelessness and Susan’s mother’s waiting are reported matter-of-factly, so the reader’s expectations are lowered before the long effort begins. Third, it structures the crisis as a sequence of setbacks rather than a single blow: a difficult labour, a lifeless child, a mother in danger, and then the long stretch in which nothing improves.

Fourth, it controls emotional register: the grief and the fear belong to the household, the analysis belongs to Manson, and the narration itself stays level — clinical terms, measured durations, no wailing and no rhetoric. That separation prevents the scene from becoming sentimental and allows the ending to arrive as feeling rather than as declaration. Students writing on tension should quote one procedural detail, name the limitation it imposes, and say how the sequence of setbacks shapes the reader’s expectations — the standard three-move answer for this text.

questions.prompt: Describe the crisis at the Morgan house. Give four details.
questions.answer: Four details are: Andrew Manson is called late at night to a household where Susan Morgan is in labour with her first child after twenty years of marriage; after a long and difficult labour the baby is born lifeless, showing no signs of breathing; Susan herself is in danger, so there are two emergencies at once; and the midwife, who is practical and experienced, loses hope while Susan’s mother can only wait, so Manson is left as the sole source of action in the room.
questions.explanation: Four distinct details covering the household, the child, the mother and the witnesses are required.

questions.prompt: How does the story show Manson’s perseverance?
questions.answer: It shows it through conduct rather than declaration. Faced with a still child and a hopeful room that has given up, he orders hot and cold water baths, chest compression and artificial respiration and keeps the sequence going for over thirty minutes although nothing improves and the midwife’s judgment stands against him. He also divides a crisis rather than choosing the easier path — treating Susan with an injection first and then returning to the child — which shows discipline alongside endurance. And he begins the night distracted by personal concerns, sets them aside entirely, and continues to the point of physical and emotional exhaustion, so his persistence is a choice he renews rather than an impulse he feels.
questions.explanation: The answer must cite the repeated methods with their duration, the prioritisation of the mother, and the setting aside of his own distractions.

questions.prompt: How does Cronin build suspense in this story? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: Cronin builds suspense first by limiting the field. The action occupies one house, late at night, in a small mining town where no other help can be summoned quickly, so every option the doctor has is one he must supply himself. Second, he lowers expectations before the main effort begins: the labour has already been long, the baby is born lifeless, the midwife’s practical judgement declares the child beyond saving, and Susan’s mother can do nothing but wait — so when Manson starts work, the reader believes the odds are against him. Third, the crises arrive in sequence rather than at once — a difficult delivery, a lifeless child, a mother in danger — and the doctor’s attention must move between them, which means each solved problem immediately exposes the next. Fourth, suspense is carried by procedure and measurement: the methods are named (hot and cold baths, chest compression, artificial respiration) and the time is counted (over thirty minutes), so tension lives in the duration of unchanging evidence rather than in dramatic speech. Fifth, the narration’s register stays level — the emotion belongs to the room, not the prose — and that gap between calm description and rising stakes is what makes the reader anxious. The climax is then prepared rather than sprung: the cry arrives at the precise moment Manson is about to give up, releasing the tension at its highest point. Answers should quote one procedural detail and one structural feature, because this story’s tension is engineered through method, limitation and sequence, and general statements about drama will not show the mechanism.
questions.explanation: Full marks require at least three devices named with textual illustration, and an account of how the sequence of setbacks positions the reader for the climax.

questions.prompt: Is the title Birth about the baby, or about the doctor? Discuss with evidence from the whole story.
questions.answer: The case for the baby is literal and unavoidable: the chapter records a delivery — a long labour, a child born lifeless, and a struggle in which that child is brought into the world against apparent finality. Nearly every detail of the plot serves this reading: the midwife’s hope, the mother’s danger, the methods applied to the infant, and the cry that announces life. On this reading the title names the event, and the story’s achievement is to make a single delivery as tense as a plot, through procedural detail and the narrowing of options in a small-town house at night. The case for the doctor rests on what the story emphasises after the event. The narration is close to Manson throughout, and the emotional climax is his, not the household’s: the words “I’ve done something… something real at last” are his recognition, and they answer a question the opening had already raised, because he began the night distracted, unsure and at the start of a career in which nothing had yet been tested. The story also withholds any external reward — no praise, no reputation, no consequence beyond the room — so what the night produces is internal: a vocation confirmed. The parallel structure then completes the doubling: the child enters life as Manson enters his working life, and the same thirty minutes accomplish both. The balanced judgement is that the two readings are the same event described at different scales — a birth is a beginning, and Cronin chooses the one beginning that can stand for the other, which is why the title is a single word carrying two subjects. The best answers will quote the closing line and one procedural passage, showing that the event on the page is literal while the story’s interest has quietly moved to the man performing it.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings evidenced, attention to the opening’s distracted doctor and the closing line as an arc, and a judgement explaining why the double title is one event rather than two.
